title: Moral Disengagement
description: A set of mental tricks that allow people to do harmful things without feeling guilt or seeing themselves as bad people. They reframe the action, the victim, or their own responsibility until the immoral act feels acceptable.

sections.title: What It Is
sections.content: A set of mental tricks that allow people to do harmful things without feeling guilt or seeing themselves as bad people. They reframe the action, the victim, or their own responsibility until the immoral act feels acceptable.

sections.title: How It Actually Appears
content: A manager lays off workers and calls it “right‑sizing” or “optimizing resources.”
A bully says, “It was just a joke; they’re too sensitive.”
Soldiers dehumanize enemy combatants by using slurs, making it easier to harm them.
A company pollutes a river but argues “we provide jobs, so it balances out.”

sections.title: Common Behaviors
content: Euphemistic language: “collateral damage” for civilian deaths.
Displacement of responsibility: “I was just following orders.”
Diffusion of responsibility: “Everyone was doing it.”
Blaming the victim: “They brought it on themselves.”

sections.title: Real Phrases
content: “It’s just business.”
“They had it coming.”
“Compared to what others do, this is nothing.”
“You can’t make an omelet without breaking eggs.”

sections.title: Warning Signs
content: You hear someone justify a harmful act with language that softens it.
They refer to people as categories, not individuals.
They minimize consequences or shift focus to their good intentions.
They act as if they had no choice.

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Albert Bandura (1999) identified eight mechanisms of moral disengagement. They allow people to maintain a positive self‑image while violating their own moral standards. It’s the psychology of “good people doing bad things.”

sections.title: Protection Strategy
content: Call it what it is. When you hear a euphemism, replace it with plain language: “You fired 200 people, not ‘right‑sized.’”
Hold individuals accountable by name. Moral disengagement thrives in vagueness.
Ask: “If this happened to you or your family, would you still call it that?”

sections.title: Common Mistakes
content: Assuming moral disengagement only applies to war criminals. It’s in every office, school, and family.
Using these mechanisms yourself without realizing it. Self‑audit your justifications.

sections.title: Real Scenario
sections.content: A marketing team launches a campaign targeting children with sugary snacks. When confronted, the team says, “Parents are the real decision‑makers,” and “It’s just a fun ad.” They have morally disengaged by displacing responsibility and using euphemisms for exploitation.

sections.title: Key Insight
sections.content: When the words feel clean, the action is probably dirty. If you need a sanitized phrase to describe what you did, you already know it was wrong.
